title: Casper and the Language
premise: Xanthe Thackeray has spent four years writing postcards to their late mother at an address that no longer exists, unable to grieve a woman they both loved and resented. At the funeral of Aunt Delphine, the family's last anchor, a stranger named Casper greets the mourners using 'the Language' — a private family dialect invented by Xanthe's grandmother and thought to have died with her. Casper, it emerges, was the grandmother's undocumented caretaker and, perhaps, her unacknowledged son. As Xanthe teaches Casper the words he only half-knows and he forces them to finally read their mother's last unsent letter aloud, the two forge a fragile found family built on shared grief. The novel ends with Xanthe mailing one final postcard — addressed to themselves, in the Language — choosing ownership of their own life over tenancy in the past.
about_author: Orsen Okonkwo is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing undelivered letters in a provincial postal dead-letter office before turning to fiction. He writes about inheritance, invented languages, and the families we assemble from strangers.

chapters.title: Poste Restante
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. We meet Xanthe through their ritual: weekly postcards to a burned-down house, written in fragments of a private family language nobody else speaks. Their flat feels rented, their life provisional. Emotional beat: quiet, self-aware loneliness; the reader senses grief deferred, not resolved.

chapters.title: The Funeral of Delphine Thackeray
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At Aunt Delphine's sparsely attended funeral, Xanthe performs the role of composed heir while cousins argue over the estate. A stranger in a grey coat stands at the back and weeps openly. Emotional beat: performative composure cracking under the weight of being the last Thackeray who remembers anything.

chapters.title: A Word Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The stranger approaches and greets Xanthe with 'seluneth' — a word from the Language meaning roughly 'homecoming.' No living person should know it. He introduces himself as Casper and refuses to explain further. Emotional beat: vertigo; the past reaching into the present through a single syllable.

chapters.title: Casper
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. We learn his history: hired as a teenager to tend the grandmother's garden, he absorbed the Language she taught him, and stayed twenty years as companion, confidant, and possibly more. Delphine paid him to stay away after the grandmother died. Emotional beat: tender, guilty devotion; a man shaped entirely by someone else's family.

chapters.title: The Estate Inventory
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Sorting Delphine's house, Xanthe and Casper find the grandmother's notebooks: the Language fully documented, plus letters suggesting Casper was her son, given away young. Neither says it aloud. Emotional beat: discovery as excavation; every object is evidence of love that had to hide itself.

chapters.title: Lessons
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe begins teaching Casper the words he never learned, and he corrects Xanthe's rusty grammar. Sessions become confession: Xanthe admits they never said goodbye to their mother, whose final letter remains sealed. Emotional beat: intimacy growing through vocabulary; teaching as a form of touch.

chapters.title: The Cousins Object
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. The extended family discovers Casper's claim on the estate and accuses him of con artistry, threatening legal action. Xanthe defends him publicly, burning bridges with the only blood relatives they have left. Emotional beat: love against duty; Xanthe chooses the stranger who carries their memory over the family that carries their name.

chapters.title: Seluneth
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Cornered by lawyers and doubting himself, Casper prepares to leave. Xanthe finds him packing and, for the first time, reads the mother's letter aloud — in the Language — discovering it names him. The word 'seluneth' appears in it: homecoming. Emotional beat: climax; grief spoken out loud at last, transforming both of them.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The will is finally read: Delphine left the house not to the cousins but to whoever would keep the Language alive. Xanthe and Casper inherit it together, along with the truth of the grandmother's choices. Emotional beat: bittersweet vindication; legitimacy granted too late to matter, yet mattering anyway.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Months later, Xanthe writes one last postcard — to themself, at their own address, in fluent Language — and mails it. Casper plants the grandmother's roses. The house is lived in now, owned, warm. Emotional beat: resolution; memory honored not by dwelling in it but by speaking it forward into a chosen future.
